title: Momentum conservation for ab initio calculations with pseudopotentials via a phase space electronic structure formulation
authors: Guy Ohad, Nadine C. Bradbury, Joseph E. Subotnik
abstract: We demonstrate how to build a robust phase space electronic Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_\text{PS}(\boldsymbol{R},\boldsymbol{P})$ that depends on nuclear position $\boldsymbol{R}$ and nuclear momentum $\boldsymbol{P}$ in the presence of ionic pseudopotentials. In particular, we show that in order to account for the non-local component of a pseudopotential while also conserving linear and angular momentum, one is forced to introduce a non-local one-electron operator $\hat{\boldsymbolΓ}^\text{nl}$ that couples electronic and nuclear momenta together. To test the validity of our ansatz, we derive a generalized form of Nafie's exact equality (which relates electronic momentum and electronic position) so as to include the presence of pseudopotentials. We then benchmark our proposed phase space electronic structure theory against this generalized Nafie-like result for a diverse set of diatomic molecules spanning a wide range of elements. We find excellent agreement across this ab initio test set, highlighting the strength of our method in capturing meaningful electronic momentum beyond the Born-Oppenheimer framework.
summary: This paper develops a robust phase space electronic Hamiltonian to correctly model molecular dynamics while incorporating pseudopotentials. By introducing a non-local operator, the authors ensure the conservation of linear and angular momentum, which is crucial for accurate non-adiabatic calculations. Benchmarking against a generalized Nafie's equality confirms the method's success in capturing electronic momentum beyond the standard Born-Oppenheimer approximation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing a phase space electronic Hamiltonian that correctly conserves linear and angular momentum when incorporating pseudopotentials into *ab initio* calculations.
main_result: The proposed phase space theory successfully captures meaningful electronic momentum beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, demonstrated by excellent agreement with a generalized Nafie-like equality across various diatomic molecules.
method: The authors construct a phase space Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{PS}(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{P})$ by introducing a non-local operator $\hat{\Gamma}_{nl}$ to ensure momentum conservation, and benchmark this against a generalized Nafie's equality.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to electronic structure calculations for diatomic molecules using DFT at the GGA level, extending the framework beyond the standard Born-Oppenheimer approximation to include nuclear momentum $\mathbf{P}$.
key_observables: Electronic momentum, total linear and angular momentum ($\Pi_{tot}, \Lambda_{tot}$), and the Nafie ratio (which should approach 1).
important_parameters: The non-local component of the pseudopotential ($\hat{\eta}_{nl}$), and the ratio of nuclear momenta ($\log_{10}|P_{Li}/P_{F}|$).
main_assumptions: The primary approximation involves using an approximate one-electron operator $\hat{\Gamma}_I$ to handle the non-local pseudopotentials, and the analysis often restricts itself to single-atom translations to maintain a well-defined diagnostic ratio.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the Nafie ratio for 17 diatomic molecules using the approximate phase space operator. Figure 3 plots the Nafie ratio for vibrating LiF versus the ratio of nuclear momenta, showing convergence to 1 in limits. Figure 4 compares the ratio when the non-local pseudopotential term is included versus excluded.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the need for a phase space Hamiltonian to conserve momentum beyond BO. It details the construction of the Hamiltonian using a non-local operator $\hat{\Gamma}_{nl}$. The core of the work involves deriving and testing a generalized Nafie's equality, benchmarking the theory against this diagnostic using multiple diatomic systems.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and open quantum systems because it provides a rigorous, momentum-conserving framework for molecular dynamics calculations that explicitly accounts for the non-adiabatic coupling effects inherent in pseudopotentials, moving beyond simple BO treatments.
